4c755521eabec7e1: CAPE TOWN: Josh Inglis and Alex Carey added an unbeaten 145 for the fifth wicket as Australia took a first innings lead on the second day of the third Test against South Africa at Newlands on Wednesday.
Australia were 330 for four at the close, one run ahead of South Africa's first innings total of 329 with six wickets remaining.
Matt Renshaw and Cameron Green contributed 126 for the third wicket before Inglis and Carey put Australia into a strong position to push for victory in the series-deciding match.

Australia's progress on a good batting pitch was twice interrupted by double strikes by the South African bowlers but it was their only success as they toiled on an unresponsive pitch on a warm, cloudless day.

Asked whether the absence through a neck injury of star batsman Steve Smith had inspired an extra degree of responsibility for the other Australia batsmen, Renshaw said there had been no such discussion.
"It was more just how could we stick to our tempo, stick to our plans and try and see where we were going to be tonight," said Renshaw.
Renshaw, restored to the top of the order after excelling at number five in the first Test, said each batsman had his own tempo and said "calmness" was another key factor.
Renshaw and Travis Head (41) shared Australia's best opening partnership of the series, putting on 58 before Head chopped off-spinner Simon Harmer's first ball of the match into his stumps.
Harmer followed up five balls later by having Marnus Labuschagne caught at slip without scoring.
- Calmer heads prevail -
Renshaw (74) and Green (65) got Australia back on track but both were dismissed by left-arm fast bowler Marco Jansen in the space of three deliveries shortly before tea.

"I was in for probably an hour and a half before Cam came in so I'm at a completely different mindset and tempo compared to when he was coming in," said Renshaw. "He's buzzing around a lot so it's just about me being the calmer head out there."
Renshaw's watchful 139-ball innings ended when he flashed at a lifting delivery and was caught behind, with South Africa successfully seeking a review after he was initially given not out.

Green's more adventurous innings ended when he steered Jansen to second slip. Green, who returned from an abdominal injury, hit two sixes off successive balls from Kagiso Rabada as well as eight fours in facing 110 deliveries.
Inglis, who also missed the first two Tests because of a broken finger, played some fine attacking strokes as he made 85 not out off 111 balls.
"We were under a little bit of pressure having lost two quick wickets and the way that he played was really positive," said Renshaw.
Inglis and wicketkeeper Carey (51 not out) batted through to the close as South Africa were made to regret their collapse from 203 for one on the first day.

It was a tough day for the South African bowlers, although Jansen reached 100 wickets in only his 24th Test on the day that the International Cricket Council announced he had moved to the top of the Test rankings for both bowlers and all-rounders.

But new ball partner Rabada struggled with stomach cramps, according to bowling coach Piet Botha, and conceded 81 runs off 18 overs. Early in the afternoon he was hit for two sixes and a four off successive balls by Green. - AFP

dc3b5f8078c51bbd: SEOUL, Oct 29 — A few seconds of real-life tragedy have landed Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 in controversy, after players discovered footage from South Korea’s deadly 2022 Itaewon crowd crush embedded in a cinematic sequence depicting a fictional North Korean invasion.

The footage, showing a rescuer performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a victim of the disaster, has sparked outrage among bereaved families and civic groups, who are demanding that publisher Activision remove it from the blockbuster first-person shooter.
The controversy comes as South Korea marks the fourth anniversary today of the October 29, 2022, disaster, which claimed 159 lives during Halloween festivities in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district.
According to The Korea Times, the game initially attracted attention in South Korea for its realistic depiction of the country under attack by North Korean forces.
But that attention quickly turned to criticism when players recognised footage of the real disaster in a sequence portraying civilian casualties from the game’s fictional conflict.
The clip, lasting about three seconds, appears in the game’s opening cinematic, which uses news-style footage to establish the scale of the imagined invasion.
For families who lost loved ones in Itaewon, the use of actual rescue scenes as material for a fictional war was deeply distressing.
In a joint statement issued yesterday, the council representing bereaved families and a coalition of supporting civic groups condemned the footage and called for its immediate removal.

“We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes of citizens performing CPR to save one another, with victims lying on the cold streets, were used unchanged to create a scene in a game,” the groups said.
Activision, responding to the criticism, acknowledged that real news footage had been incorporated into the game’s opening sequence.

The company told Yonhap News Agency that the footage was intended to help convey the game’s fictional narrative, rather than reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-life tragedy.
However, the publisher did not say whether it would remove the controversial footage, leaving the families’ demands unresolved.
6355b556925cf62e: KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 691 teachers need immediate psychological interventions following a nationwide screening of 82,126 educators by the Education Ministry.

Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said the Psychological Well-Being Inventory (IKPsi) findings showed 636 teachers were at a moderate level, 32 at a moderately low level, and 23 at a low level.
She said the group accounted for 0.84 per cent of the total number of teachers screened.
However, she said the vast majority, or 99.16 per cent, recorded good psychological well-being, comprising 50,869 teachers at a high level and 30,566 at a moderately high level.

"Overall, these findings show that the majority of teachers who underwent screening are at a good level of psychological well-being, but the ministry will continue to provide attention and intervention to teachers identified as needing support.

"To assist teachers facing these challenges, the ministry implements a comprehensive intervention approach covering developmental, preventive, and rehabilitative aspects through psychological and counselling services.

"Among the services provided are individual and group counselling, psychological testing, guidance and consultation, as well as stress management programmes and emotional support for ministry personnel," she said in a written reply published on the parliament website.

She was responding to a question from Datuk Muslimin Yahya (PN-Sungai Besar) on the number of teachers facing health problems and mental disorders, as well as the intervention measures and support assistance provided by the ministry to help them sustain their lives and careers.
Fadhlina said the intervention approach begins with screening and identifying individual needs, followed by suitable psychological and counselling interventions.

"Among the intervention measures implemented are those focusing on individual issues and needs, covering financial management, serious indebtedness, moderate performance, and mental health-related issues.
"In crises, the support provided through intervention can help individuals stabilise their emotions, identify strengths and support resources, and develop an action plan to restore functioning.

"The ministry's approach not only focuses on resolving current issues, but also strengthens the capacity of teachers to maintain long-term well-being. This effort aims to help teachers regain stability and function well, enabling them to pursue their lives and careers more resiliently," she said.

Apart from psychological and counselling interventions, the ministry is also upgrading staffrooms with a total allocation of RM200 million, including an additional RM100 million, to support educators' welfare.
"This initiative aims to provide more comfortable workspaces, improved basic amenities, and a conducive, professional atmosphere to support teachers' needs in performing their daily duties.

"Providing a suitable work environment not only improves the comfort and convenience of teachers, but also supports their physical, emotional, and psychological well-being in carrying out their responsibilities effectively.

"This effort aligns with the ministry's comprehensive approach to teachers' well-being, including preparing a work environment that fosters a positive, harmonious work atmosphere and supports their productivity and motivation," she said.

Fadhlina said the ministry would continue to strengthen psychological and counselling services, and roll out appropriate interventions based on the needs of education personnel to safeguard teachers' psychological well-being continuously.

e5df1e8b563bb2f8: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — Bursa Malaysia opened higher for the third consecutive day today tracking overnight gains on Wall Street after the United States Federal Reserve (Fed) kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75 per cent to 4.00 per cent.
At 9.10 am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 4.71 points, or 0.29 per cent, to 1,618.58 from yestereday’s close of 1,613.87.
The benchmark index opened 0.57 of a point higher at 1,614.44.

Turnover stood at 173.26 million units worth RM74.17 million.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the Fed’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged was widely expected, although concerns over persistent inflation remain.
On the home front, he said the benchmark index is gradually stabilising, although subdued trading activity suggests that investors remain selective.
“Nonetheless, we expect bargain hunting to continue among fundamentally sound banking, technology and plantation counters.
“Hence, for today, we envisage the benchmark index hovering within the 1,610-1,620 range,” he told Bernama.

Among the heavyweight stocks, Maybank rose one sen to RM10.00, while Public Bank and CIMB each rose three sen to RM4.74 and RM7.14. Tenaga Nasional added 10 sen to RM13.32, while IHH Healthcare was flat at RM7.83.

In active trade, Zetrix AI and Land & General were flat at 8.5 sen and 19 sen, respectively. Kanger International slid half a sen to one sen. CTOS Digital increased three sen to 42 sen, while Iconic Worldwide rose half a sen to 12 sen.

Among the top losers, United Plantations lost 16 sen to RM29.16, while LPI Capital declined four sen to RM13.04. Spritzer and Hap Seng Plantations shed three sen each to RM3.66 and RM2.22. QL Resources slid two sen to RM3.78.

d427f6a191628b00: MIAMI: Lionel Messi's Inter Miami stumbled to a 2-2 draw with Cincinnati on Wednesday in an MLS game that sprang to life after half-time with four superb goals.

Miami took the lead with a Luis Suarez strike on the hour mark, but conceded two in quick succession before grabbing back a late equalizer from substitute Riquelme Fillipi to ensure the spoils were shared.
The draw was a setback in Miami's pursuit of the Eastern Conference's second seed, as the star-studded side lost ground on the New England Revolution, who beat the New York Red Bulls 3-2.

Despite the heartbreak of Fillipi's late strike, the point could prove valuable for Cincinnati, who sit on the cusp of the automatic playoff places, but are currently headed for the wild card round and could yet miss out entirely with two games remaining.
In a low-key first half, Miami controlled possession and comprehensively out-passed Cincinnati, but were unable to pierce through.
That changed in the 61st minute, as Rodrigo De Paul picked up the ball in the middle of the park, in acres of space, and played it wide to Casemiro.
The Brazilian played it first time with the outside of his boot to Suarez, lurking just inside the box.
The Uruguayan veteran took one touch, swiveled and perfectly curled the ball into the far top corner, where it crashed down and in off the crossbar.
But Cincinnati rallied, and in the 80th minute Frenchman Kenji Mboma Dem scored with another beautiful curling effort to the far post.
He picked up the ball wide right, ran at multiple defenders with a flurry of stepovers, then cut inside to score.
Just six minutes later, Cincinnati silenced Miami's Nu Stadium by taking the lead.
Defender Samuel Gidi received a pass on the edge of the box and wrapped his left foot around the ball, sending it past Dayne St. Clair.

With Messi heavily man-marked and unable to get a shot away, De Paul sprayed a wide pass to young Brazilian attacker Fillipi, who cut back to the corner of the box and bent it through two defenders and into the far side of the goal.

Both sides had even later chances to win the game, with Suarez blasting his at the goalkeeper before Evander's shot was blocked by a defender at close range as the referee waved away handball appeals.
Inter Miami play New England on Sunday, sitting two points back and needing either a win or a draw to keep their hopes of second place alive.
Nashville SC are top, and clinched the Supporters' Shield last weekend for the first time in the club's history. — AFP
3a912dc94e27fbdb: RIO DE JANEIRO: Santos captain Neymar has been handed a two-match suspension for covering his mouth while arguing with an opponent during Saturday's 1-1 Brazilian Serie A draw with Bahia, Brazil's Superior Court of Sports Justice (STJD) said on Wednesday.

The 34-year-old was sent off following an altercation with Bahia midfielder Rodrigo Nestor, and the sports tribunal found him guilty of violating the Vinicius Jr. rule that forbids players from covering their mouths during on-field confrontations.
The STJD said the referee's report also noted that Neymar, after being sent off, ran towards the visitors' bench to confront his opponent and had to be restrained by teammates.

The suspension means Neymar will miss Santos' next three matches. He is already banned for Wednesday's league game against Palmeiras after accumulating three yellow cards and will serve two additional matches for the protocol violation.
Neymar and Santos can appeal the ruling regarding the violation.

The latest suspension comes three months after Neymar became the first player in Brazil's top flight to be temporarily removed from the field under a new rule being tested in the league to curb time-wasting by goalkeepers.
The former Brazil captain is not expected to return to action until late November. - Reuters

dab67996e4042585: SINGAPORE, Oct 29 — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Indonesia President Prabowo Subianto have held high-level communication amid recent bilateral challenges.

Singapore Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan said the communication has established political commitment on both sides to do “what is necessary,” and that the focus now is to implement and execute the plans and commitment.

Balakrishnan described his visit to Jakarta as also involving engagement at the highest level, having met his newly appointed counterpart, Indonesia Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir, as well as having called on Prabowo.
“We had good conversations, honest conversations, sincere conversations, and we have come up with a few constructive approaches, some of which we are in the midst of implementing.

Balakrishnan said their announcement yesterday (Tuesday) on the Joint Task Force “is a recognition that in the case of haze, it is a transboundary problem and it requires a collegiate, collective response on the part of both Indonesia and Singapore.”

The minister said the task force aims to facilitate a collective response, enhance information sharing, and strengthen coordination to deter companies engaging in such anti-social and, frankly, dangerous acts.
“We can also hold them accountable, and we can try our best to make sure that this does not recur,” he added. — Bernama

68103331303f6f36: MUNICH: Bayern Munich sporting director Max Eberl said Wednesday coach Vincent Kompany had been discharged from hospital, revealing the Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation.
Kompany was rushed to hospital after collapsing on the training pitch in Munich on Friday, with Bayern saying the coach was suffering from a virus.
Speaking minutes before Bayern's last-32 German Cup tie with Magdeburg, Eberl told ARD the doctors had determined the cause of the illness and had discharged the 40-year-old Kompany.
"We have identified the cause: it is a case of meningeal irritation, which is what triggered the incident last Friday," Eberl said.
On Saturday, Bayern said it was a matter of "weeks, not days" until Kompany returned to the dugout, with English assistant coach Aaron Danks taking over in his absence.
After Sunday's 3-1 win at Freiburg, Danks said the coaching staff would avoid talking football with the ailing Kompany during his recovery.
"He has now been allowed to go home, where he can continue his rehabilitation," Eberl said on Wednesday.
"For him, rehabilitation means rest and medication. I am very, very confident that he will be back on the touchline at 100 percent very soon."
"I believe it is the best and most wonderful news for all of us," Eberl said.

Kompany was visibly sick and walked with a limp during Bayern's 6-1 home win over RB Leipzig in mid-October. He was in doubt for their home clash with Arsenal four days later, but took to the dugout for the 2-2 draw, two days before his training-pitch collapse. - AFP
61f63a57430cbcf2: SYDNEY: England face their earliest Rugby League World Cup exit ever this weekend with their fate in the hands of Tonga and Samoa during bumper games that will decide the semi-final line-up.

Ahead of the last group matches defending champions Australia are the only side to have secured a final-four berth while France, Lebanon and the Cook Islands have been eliminated from the 10-team tournament.
New Zealand face Fiji on Australia's Gold Coast on Saturday with the winner joining the Kangaroos from Group A.
The permutations for Groups B and C are more complicated with only two of the six nations from a combined table staying alive.
World number three England must emphatically beat Papua New Guinea on Friday in Wollongong then await the fate of a crunch Tonga-Samoa clash in Sydney on Sunday.
If Samoa win, Brian McDermott's men will make their first group-stage exit in World Cup history, given they would be level on points with Tonga but with an inferior head-to-head record.
Should Tonga beat their Pacific rivals, the Tongans would top the table and England's fate would come down to points difference with Samoa, who are currently in a much better position.
Nevertheless England half-back Mikey Lewis said their hopes were high.
"We're in with a fighting chance, we believe that," said the Hull KR star. "We feel it in these four walls."
Tonga lost 34-6 to Samoa at the same Sydney stadium during the Pacific Championships last year.
But coach Kristian Woolf said they had come a long way since, pointing to their 30-12 upset of England to open their World Cup.
"There's no doubt Australia, New Zealand and England are still the tier one nations," Woolf said.
"They're the biggest nations, they've got the biggest player pools and the best resources.
"But we're closing the gap. At this tournament we see ourselves as equal."
New Zealand have recalled centre Dane Gagai and prop Moses Leota, who were rested last week, for their blockbuster winner-takes-all showdown against Fiji.
But coming off a battling 36-22 loss to Australia last week, Fiji captain Api Koroisau is confident his young side can upset the Kiwis.
"I thought we were actually on top of that first-half (against Australia) and had some really good field position and the confidence is really high," he said.
"I think it's just really driven that belief into the boys knowing that they can do it."
In the women's World Cup, which is being held concurrently, Australia are through to the semi-finals after big wins over Samoa and England.
Samoa and England face each other on Friday with the winner joining the Jillaroos, while victory for New Zealand over Papua New Guinea will also see them progress.
A win for Fiji over France should be enough for them to advance, although it could come down to points difference if PNG upset New Zealand. — AFP

ccb2327fc2b96335: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today expressed deep grief over the tragic loss of lives in the train collision in Spain.
In a Facebook post, he said however Malaysia stood in solidarity with the people of Spain at this difficult time.
“Our thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones, and we wish the injured a swift recovery,” he said.
Anwar also paid tribute to the emergency personnel and others working tirelessly at the scene.

“On behalf of the Government and people of Malaysia, I extend our deepest condolences to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, the Government and people of Spain, and especially to the families of the victims,” prime minister said.

b11e7a83f66e066f: KUALA LUMPUR: The government's petroleum subsidy bill is projected to reach RM40 billion this year as a global supply crisis pushes crude oil prices above US$120 per barrel.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said monthly subsidies for petrol, diesel and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) surged from about RM800 million in January and February to nearly RM5 billion in March and April.
However, the monthly subsidy burden eased to about RM3 billion between June and August.
Anwar, who is also finance minister, said the government had adopted a balanced approach to protect Malaysians from rising fuel prices while safeguarding the country's fiscal sustainability.
"The government has reprioritised its annual expenditure to focus on programmes that deliver the greatest impact to the people and the economy.

"This exercise takes into account the operational needs and priorities of each ministry, particularly to ensure that high-impact programmes and essential services, including education, healthcare and financial assistance, remain protected," he said in a written parliamentary reply.
He was responding to Datuk Seri Mohd Shafie Apdal (Warisan-Semporna), who sought details on petroleum subsidies.

Anwar said the government would strengthen fiscal discipline by tightening operating expenditure, improving public spending efficiency and reducing leakages in the implementation of programmes and subsidies.
"Enforcement activities have also been stepped up to ensure government assistance and subsidies reach those who are genuinely eligible, thereby optimising the use of public funds.

"The government will continue to balance the need to protect Malaysians from rising fuel prices with prudent expenditure management to ensure higher subsidy costs can be absorbed without compromising the country's fiscal sustainability," he added.
d22389ca91cd69d6: SINGAPORE: The US dollar steadied on Thursday after the Federal Reserve held interest rates as expected while hinting upcoming inflation data would influence future policy moves, leaving investors uncertain about the rates outlook.

The Fed opted to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's midterm election in a 10-2 decision, which came with an upgraded assessment of an economy that the central bank now says is growing at a "strong pace".

That, along with the confidence expressed by Fed chair Kevin Warsh that inflation can be lowered to the 2% target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment, pushed traders to rein in bets for rate hikes in 2027.

The euro eased 0.15% to US$1.1134 in early Asian hours after the common currency firmed 0.3% in the previous session following the Fed decision. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar was up 0.14% at ¥158.045.
The greenback had held near two-week highs ahead of the announcement but turned lower after Warsh's press conference offered no clear steer on a December move.
"Warsh's silence on further rate hikes was interpreted as dovish, or not hawkish enough," said Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
"Some market participants might have expected him to pair the on-hold decision with a little bit of guidance on the December meeting, but he didn't do that."
Traders are pricing in a 78% chance of a hike in December, the FedWatch tool showed. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of six currencies, was at 102.26.

The Treasury yield curve steepened after Warsh started his press conference, with the 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with Fed interest rate expectations, falling as low as 4.678%. It was last down 2.3 basis points at 4.712% in Asian hours.
Kerry Craig, global market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management, said the meeting outcome gave the market and the Fed time to assess upcoming jobs and inflation data.

"The market reaction today was dovish... However, with policy tightening already being priced in, this implies that yields will remain range-bound unless there is a clearer signal for more aggressive policy tightening or a pivot to cuts," Craig said.

Warsh said on ​Wednesday the central bank would begin setting aside one of its eight regularly scheduled policy meetings next year and ‌two in 2028 to weigh major issues facing the institution and would not use them to consider changes in monetary policy.

"The changing of meeting schedules for 2027 and 2028, where one and two of the eight meetings will discuss strategy not policy changes, respectively, reads as dovish to us," analysts at TD Securities said in a note. "It may also have the side effect of producing potentially both more extreme and more inter-meeting moves down the line."

Attention now shifts to central bank meetings in Europe and Japan. The European Central Bank will announce its decision later on Thursday, while the Bank of Japan concludes a two-day meeting on Friday. Both central banks are expected to leave interest rates unchanged.
"Barring major hawkish surprises at either of those meetings, we would expect the dollar to continue to consolidate towards the top of recent ranges," ING analysts said.

The New Zealand dollar stabilised on Thursday at 0.5621 per dollar, after it had slumped as much as 1.7% after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand unexpectedly held interest rates at 2.75%, in a decision that stunned markets.
The Australian dollar was last at US$0.705, hovering near a one-month high.

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate for the first time in more than three years and said further increases ​might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from fuelling inflation. The Canadian dollar last bought 1.399 per US dollar.

07ca7e888ed0f67b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — The decline of reading culture and the rise of shallow thinking in the digital age are pressing challenges that could threaten the future of civilisation, says Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

In a Facebook post yesterday, the prime minister shared his thoughts after taking time to read the latest work by James Marriott, titled The New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society.

He said the threat to civilisation does not stem from a loss of access to knowledge — of which there is now a glut — but from society’s waning love and patience for reading, reflecting, and thinking critically and deeply.
“We may be increasingly wealthy in information, yet impoverished in wisdom. The question, therefore, is not merely whether humanity still reads, but whether humanity still wants to think,” he said.

Reflecting on history, Anwar recalled society’s deep reverence for intellectual and literary traditions upon the death of great French writer Victor Hugo in 1885, which saw around two million people gather in Paris to pay their last respects.

He said a similar scene unfolded following the death of renowned Russian literary giant Fyodor Dostoevsky in 1881, when tens of thousands joined his funeral procession in Saint Petersburg, demonstrating how deeply society at the time valued literature, culture, intellectual traditions, and thought.
“Neither of them was a king nor a victorious warlord, but they were thinkers and scholars whose ideas resonated deeply in the hearts and minds of society,” he added. — Bernama
41b400c55024795e: OCTOBER 29 — Imagine a university student being accused of academic dishonesty for using artificial intelligence (AI) to improve an assignment. Now imagine the same assignment being marked by a lecturer who uses AI to generate feedback, suggest grades or evaluate the student’s arguments. The student is expected to declare every use of AI, but the lecturer may not be required to explain anything. Is this academic integrity, or are we practising double standards?

This is an uncomfortable question Malaysian universities must confront. We cannot continue treating AI as a threat when students use it and a symbol of innovation when lecturers do. If universities want students to behave ethically, lecturers must demonstrate the same responsibility.

Let us be clear. AI is not the enemy of education. Blind dependence on it is. A student who copies an AI-generated essay without thinking has learned very little. Equally, a lecturer who accepts AI-generated marks or comments without carefully reviewing them has neglected an important professional responsibility.

The solution is not to ban AI but to rethink how we teach, learn and assess. We can learn from universities abroad. The University of Sydney in Australia has introduced a two-lane assessment approach. Some assessments are supervised to establish what students can do independently, while others openly allow AI as a learning tool. This recognises a simple reality: graduates must learn both to think for themselves and to work responsibly with technology.

Universities should require both students and lecturers to disclose how they use AI, including how it contributes to assignments or feedback, and ensure all work is personally reviewed to uphold academic integrity. — Pexels.com pic

University College London takes another important position. While it provides guidance for responsible student use of AI, its guidance states that lecturers should not use generative AI to mark students’ work because of concerns about reliability and bias. Meanwhile, guidance at the University of Minnesota encourages transparency, human review and the option of human feedback when AI is involved.

These examples offer valuable lessons for Malaysia. First, universities should introduce an AI Accountability Receipt for both students and lecturers. Students would briefly explain how AI helped them, which suggestions they rejected and what intellectual contributions were genuinely theirs. Lecturers who use AI for feedback should similarly disclose its role and confirm that they personally reviewed the work. Academic honesty must travel in both directions.

Second, we should introduce an innovative assessment called “Put AI on Trial.” Instead of asking students to write another predictable essay, give them an AI-generated answer containing questionable claims, weak arguments and possibly fabricated references. Their task is to expose the mistakes, correct the reasoning and defend their decisions. The marks should reward the student’s judgment, not the machine’s fluency.

Third, every major AI-assisted assignment could include a short “Defend Your Thinking” conversation. Students explain their choices, challenge the AI’s suggestions and demonstrate what they have learned. This need not be an intimidating oral examination. Even a three-minute discussion can reveal thinking that a polished written submission may conceal.

Fourth, lecturers must remain responsible for the marks they award. AI may help prepare rubrics, organise feedback or suggest improvements where institutional rules permit, but it should never become an unquestioned judge of student achievement. Students also deserve privacy protection, meaningful explanations of their grades and a fair opportunity to challenge errors.

Finally, fairness means ensuring that students have reasonable access to approved AI tools and proper training. Otherwise, students who can afford expensive subscriptions may gain advantages over those who cannot. Universities should assess intellectual ability, not purchasing power.

Malaysia has an opportunity to develop graduates who are not merely competent users of AI but thoughtful critics of it. This requires lecturers to model the ethical conduct they expect from students. Perhaps the real question universities should ask is no longer, “Did you use AI?” but rather, “What did you contribute that AI could not?” And lecturers must be prepared to answer that question too. We cannot teach integrity through rules that apply only to students. If AI is to transform higher education, accountability must begin on both sides of the classroom.
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
8b2faae4ac9be541: SINGAPORE: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto have held high-level talks amid recent bilateral challenges.

Singapore Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan said the communication had established political commitment on both sides to do "what is necessary", and that the focus was now on implementing and executing the plans and commitments.

"I am not at liberty to discuss the details, but just let me give you the assurance that communication has occurred at the highest level between my prime minister and with President Prabowo," he told Singapore media following the conclusion of his working visit to Indonesia on Wednesday.

He was asked about the state of bilateral relations between Singapore and Indonesia following recent developments, as well as details of his meeting with Prabowo on the same day. The transcript of the interview was made available by Singapore's Foreign Ministry.
Balakrishnan described his visit to Jakarta as involving engagement at the highest level, having met his newly appointed Indonesian counterpart, Arrmanatha Nasir, and called on Prabowo.
"We had good conversations, honest conversations, sincere conversations, and we have come up with a few constructive approaches, some of which we are in the midst of implementing."

Balakrishnan said their announcement on Tuesday on the Joint Task Force "is a recognition that in the case of haze, it is a transboundary problem and it requires a collegiate, collective response on the part of both Indonesia and Singapore".

The minister said the task force aimed to facilitate a collective response, enhance information sharing and strengthen coordination to deter companies engaging in such anti-social and, frankly, dangerous acts.
"We can also hold them accountable, and we can try our best to make sure that this does not recur," he added.

7828a72bd1fbde80: SIBU: The new Batang Paloh Bridge, a RM289.8 million project opening tomorrow, will end Pulau Bruit, Daro's reliance on ferries and mark a new chapter in the island's economic growth.

The 1.7-kilometre bridge is expected to speed up the movement of residents and the transport of agricultural and marine produce to outside markets, easing the logistical constraints that have long hampered the island's economic activity.

Deputy Premier of Sarawak and Minister of Infrastructure and Port Development Sarawak Datuk Amar Douglas Uggah Embas announced the bridge's opening at a recent sitting of the Sarawak State Legislative Assembly.

He said the Batang Paloh Bridge, together with the completed Muara Lassa Bridge, will strengthen the coastal road network and enhance Pulau Bruit's connectivity with Daro, Tanjung Manis, Sarikei and surrounding areas.

A Bernama survey found that residents welcome the bridge's opening, expected to end the hardship of waiting for ferries, especially during festive seasons and school holidays, when waits can stretch to several hours.

Kampung Semop resident Salleh Jamain, 53, said the bridge's opening is highly anticipated, as it would not only ease travel to Sibu and Sarikei but also potentially boost his income through the vehicle-repair service he runs on the side.
"I was very happy when I learnt the bridge would open at the end of the month, because trips to town will become faster and easier.
"I also did not want to miss the chance to witness this historic moment," he told Bernama.
Salleh hopes the facility will invigorate local economic activity, opening up more job opportunities and sources of income for residents.

For smallholder oil palm farmers, the bridge's opening brings even greater benefits, as deliveries of their produce to markets outside the island will no longer be subject to ferry operating schedules.
Smallholder Omarmayah Rosli said he uses four pickup trucks a day to deliver oil palm fruit to buyers in Sarikei, but the number of trips depends on ferry services.
"Right now, the number of trips is rather limited because we depend on the ferry. Once the bridge opens, we can deliver oil palm fruit at any time and make more trips.
"This will not only boost the income of smallholders but also that of workers and vehicle owners transporting the oil palm harvest," he said.

Meanwhile, Kampung Semop community chief Kamri Haron described the bridge's opening as a key turning point in Pulau Bruit's development, particularly in widening market access for agricultural and fishery produce and stimulating local business activity.
"This bridge does not merely connect Pulau Bruit to the outside world but is also a symbol of progress that opens up more economic opportunities for residents," he said. — BERNAMA
8c6b2acb0af285ce: OCTOBER 29 — All of us are mostly aware that politics used to have a predictable setting. Politicians spoke at rallies, debated in Parliament and appeared on television news. Malaysians listened, read the newspapers, occasionally, argued about what they had heard over teh tarik sessions with friends

Today, politics has found a new stage; our smartphones. It has been a mediator not only for digesting information but also reshaping how ordinary people interact with those with power. Surprisingly, nowadays it is increasingly common to discover politicians speaking casually into the camera, responding to trending issues, cracking jokes or sharing snippets of their daily lives through platforms such as Tiktok, Instagram, Facebook or YouTube.
Welcome to the age of politainment, where politics meets entertainment.

Politainment is not necessarily about turning politicians into celebrities. Rather, it describes how political information is increasingly packaged using the techniques of entertainment: personality, humour, storytelling, emotion and easily shareable content.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Today, politics has found a new stage; our smartphones. It has been a mediator not only for digesting information but also reshaping how ordinary people interact with those with power. ― AFP pic
Malaysia offers several interesting examples.

One of the current popular MPs was among the Malaysian politicians who recognised TikTok’s potential relatively early. During the 15th General Election, his account featured political speeches, campaign messages and videos designed for younger social-media audiences.

His approach demonstrates how a politician can communicate serious political messages using the language and format of a platform traditionally associated with entertainment. Instead of expecting young people to come to politics, politics goes to where young people already are.

A second example is one of the Chief Ministers of a Malaysian state whose social-media presence has become sufficiently distinctive to attract academic attention. A Malaysian study examining his TikTok content specifically describes it through the concept of politainment, analysing how political meaning is created through performance and audience interaction.

Taking him as an example, the importance of personality in contemporary political communication becomes difficult to ignore. Political messages are no longer communicated solely through manifestos and formal speeches. Humour, speaking style, spontaneity and personal image can become part of a politician’s public brand.
A third example comes from a different medium.
Two former ministers who conversed and discussed through a special podcast have demonstrated how lengthy political discussions can also adopt elements of entertainment.

The programme discusses politics, policies and current affairs in a conversational and accessible manner. Instead of the rigid atmosphere associated with a formal political interview, listeners encounter discussion, disagreement, humour and personal observations.
The podcast demonstrates how serious political issues can be presented through a conversational format that combines analysis, personal observations and humour.

These examples show that politainment is not one particular style. It can be a 30-second TikTok video, a politician cultivating an engaging online personality or a two-hour podcast discussing national issues.
There are several advantages.

Politainment can make politics accessible to people who might never watch Parliament or read lengthy policy documents. Complex issues such as the cost of living, education, employment and public transport can potentially reach larger audiences when communicated creatively.
But there is also a danger.

Social media rewards attention. Algorithms favour content that makes people watch, react, comment and share. A witty remark or confrontation can therefore travel further than a careful explanation of economic policy.
This raises an important question: Are Malaysians becoming more politically informed, or simply more politically entertained?
The distinction matters.

A politician can accumulate millions of views, likes and followers, but digital popularity alone does not tell citizens whether a policy works or whether a government decision produces the promised results.
This is where media literacy becomes crucial.
Malaysians should be able to enjoy political content while remaining critical of it. Who produced the video? What information has been omitted? Is it evidence, opinion, satire or political promotion?
Politics does not have to be boring to be meaningful. Humour, personality and storytelling can help citizens engage with important national issues.
So let’s watch the TikTok videos, listen to the podcasts and enjoy the memes.
But never neglect the policy, do check the facts and examine the records as in the age of politainment, going viral may win attention.
Ultimately. governing a country, however, requires considerably more than entertaining an audience.
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.

802f5aaefcf48f8e: SEOUL: South Korean technology giant Samsung Electronics on Thursday posted a more than 780% leap in third-quarter operating profit from a year earlier, buoyed by booming demand for AI semiconductors.
The company is the world's largest maker of memory chips - components now in huge demand as advanced types are snapped up for use in data centres powering artificial intelligence.
Samsung posted July-September operating profit at 107.4 trillion won (US$80.5 billion) - up 783.1% on-year, the company said in a regulatory filing.
It marked the first time any tech company had recorded quarterly operating profit of more than 100 trillion won, the firm said.
Net profit jumped 514.6% from last year to 75.1 trillion won, while sales reached 195.2 trillion won.
However, the results fell short of market expectations, with a Bloomberg survey of economists having predicted quarterly operating profit of 108.5 trillion won and net profit of 89.4 trillion won.
Samsung shares were were down more than 2.4% in Seoul on Thursday morning.
The global race to build AI data centres has turbocharged the fortunes of Samsung and its rivals, despite concerns that the sector may be overvalued.
The company's memory business achieved "another record-breaking quarter by managing its product mix, with a focus on AI products, amid capacity constraints," Samsung said in a statement.
"Strong demand momentum for servers led to higher market prices across all applications," it said.
38987f4b242728b8: OCTOBER 29 — According to a recent journal paper, the case for Malaysian hydrogen rests on solid fundamentals. The NETR and the Hydrogen Roadmap, both launched in 2023, identify hydrogen as a key decarbonisation lever. The country’s solar resource potential and year-round irradiance supports predictable renewable generation. In the eastern state of Sarawak, hydropower can provide a low-carbon base for electrolysis that most emerging hydrogen regions lack. The recent launch of the Malaysia Clean Hydrogen Project under the Global Clean Hydrogen Programme, executed by UNIDO with NanoMalaysia Berhad, signals that international institutions see enough promise to invest in policy and technical capacity-building over a five-year horizon.

But potential is not production. Malaysia currently generates roughly 0.6 million tonnes of hydrogen annually, mostly “grey” hydrogen derived from steam methane reforming for fertilizer, petrochemical, and electronics manufacturing. The roadmap target of 16 million tonnes by 2030 sits an order of magnitude beyond current output, and no plant currently produces hydrogen specifically for energy applications. This is not a minor gap; it is a chasm.

The economics explain why. Electricity accounts for 60 to 70 per cent of the levelised cost of hydrogen, with electrolysers adding another 20 per cent. In Peninsular Malaysia, renewable capacity remains insufficient for large-scale electrolysis, and grid wheeling charges further erode project economics. Solar contributes just over 1 percent of national electricity generation despite the country’s abundant resource, a utilisation gap that reflects land constraints, grid integration hurdles, and slow deployment. One modelling study found that in Sabah — the state with the best solar resource and land availability — the levelised cost of hydrogen could fall from US$5.81 (RM23.63) to US$2.52 per kilogram with reduced electrolyser costs, but that remains above the threshold for commercial viability without policy support.

Electricity accounts for 60 to 70 per cent of the levelised cost of hydrogen, with electrolysers adding another 20 per cent. In Peninsular Malaysia, renewable capacity remains insufficient for large-scale electrolysis, and grid wheeling charges further erode project economics. — Pexels.com pic

A separate analysis identified the “investment corridor” for hydrogen projects at costs below US$3.5 per kilogram combined with carbon taxes above US$40 per tone — a zone that current conditions do not yet reach.

Sarawak offers a partial counterpoint. With hydropower as its backbone, the state has moved further than any other Malaysian region: hydrogen refuelling stations, fuel cell buses, and announced production targets of around 10 kilotonnes per year for domestic mobility and pilot exports to Japan and South Korea. But Sarawak is an exception, and its hydropower advantage is not replicable in the peninsula, where most industrial demand and population reside.

The literature points to two underutilised domestic pathways. First, Malaysia generates millions of tonnes oil palm biomass waste annually, which could be converted to hydrogen through gasification or supercritical water gasification. This offers a near-term, waste-to-value route that leverages an existing industry rather than waiting for electrolyser cost curves to fall. Second, seawater electrolysis presents a strategically compelling option for a maritime nation: indirect seawater electrolysis is already technologically mature and would add less than US$0.1 per kilogram to the levelised cost while co-producing potable water. Direct seawater electrolysis remains at lower readiness.

The policy response has been coordination-heavy but market-light. NanoMalaysia has evolved into the government’s de facto hydrogen coordinator, convening an industry alliance to organize a fragmented private sector. The Global Clean Hydrogen Programme will strengthen standards, technical expertise, and investment preparation. Yet industry players describe a sector “pushed into existence rather than pulled forward by organic market demand”. The government’s approach of co-financing “catalytic users” to validate commercial use cases is a reasonable demand-side intervention, but it remains small in scale.

A carbon tax, now delayed, on metals, steel, and energy industries could change the calculus by making green hydrogen more competitive with grey alternatives. The real-options modelling suggests that policy clarity around carbon pricing can trigger capital deployment far earlier than traditional net-present-value analysis would predict. But a carbon tax alone will not build electrolysers or pipelines; it must be paired with cost-side reforms and infrastructure sequencing.

The strategic risk is not that Malaysia fails to become a hydrogen exporter. That ambition may be premature. The real risk is that the country spends a decade building pilot projects and roadmaps while its industrial hydrogen demand — currently met by grey production — continues to lock in carbon-intensive infrastructure that will be expensive to retrofit. The window for converting existing ammonia and petrochemical facilities to green or blue hydrogen is open now, with policy support and international climate finance. Waiting for perfect economics means waiting for competitors to capture the market first.

Malaysia’s hydrogen future will not be won in Putrajaya or Kuching alone. It will be won in Sipitang’s ammonia plants, Bintulu’s industrial clusters, and the palm oil mills of Johor — where hydrogen can become a practical input rather than a policy aspiration. The roadmaps are sound. The research is clear. The missing ingredient is urgency.

* The author is affiliated with the Tan Sri Omar Centre for STI Policy Studies at UCSI University and is an Adjunct Professor at the Ungku Aziz Centre for Development Studies, Universiti Malaya. He can be reached at ahmadibrahim@ucsiuniversity.edu.my.

Turnover stood at 173.26 million units worth RM74.17 million.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the Fed’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged was widely expected, although concerns over persistent inflation remain.

“Nonetheless, we expect bargain hunting to continue among fundamentally sound banking, technology and plantation counters.
“Hence, for today, we envisage the benchmark index hovering within the 1,610-1,620 range,” he noted.

Among the top losers, United Plantations lost 16 sen to RM29.16, while LPI Capital declined four sen to RM13.04. Spritzer and Hap Seng Plantations shed three sen each to RM3.66 and RM2.22. QL Resources slid two sen to RM3.78.

18da6d65172a8dc6: KUALA LUMPUR: Pakatan Harapan has not ruled out clashes with Bersatu in the Melaka election, despite an understanding between the two sides.
Melaka PKR acting state chairman Adam Adli Abd Halim said clashes could occur in seats beyond the seven PH has decided not to contest.

Adam Adli, who is also PKR communications director, said the coalition's decision to contest only 21 of the 28 state legislative assembly seats did not mean it deliberately vacated the remaining seven to make way for Bersatu.
"When Bersatu expressed its intention to contest in Melaka, there could be clashes between PH and the party. We decided to contest 21 seats because that matches our current capability.

"We do not want to send the wrong message, as if we deliberately vacated the seven seats for Bersatu, but it is up to them. In fact, if there are overlapping seats between PH and Bersatu, there is no problem.
"I personally expect clashes, but if Bersatu wants to play safe, they can just take those seven seats," he said in an interview with Berita Harian.
Earlier, PH announced it would contest 21 seats in the Melaka election, with PKR fielding candidates in nine seats, DAP in seven, and Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) in five.

PKR's nine state seats are Tanjung Bidara, Rembia, Asahan, Paya Rumput, Kelebang, Machap Jaya, Ayer Molek, Rim, and Serkam. DAP will contest Ayer Keroh, Kesidang, Kota Laksamana, Banda Hilir, Gadek, Duyong, and Pengkalan Batu, while Amanah will contest Kuala Linggi, Durian Tunggal, Bukit Katil, Telok Mas, and Merlimau.
The seven seats not contested by PH are Ayer Limau, Lendu, Taboh Naning, Sungai Udang, Pantai Kundor, Duyong, and Bemban.
Adam Adli, who is also the Deputy Higher Education Minister, said PH's decision to contest only 21 seats was not influenced by external parties or an electoral pact, as previously speculated.
He said Bersatu remained free to determine how many seats it wanted to contest, as no electoral pact had been established between both parties.
He said that if PH contested a seat and Bersatu also decided to field a candidate there, it was up to the party in the spirit of democracy.

"For these remaining seven seats, we do not have an electoral pact. We merely asked each other if there were seats they wished to contest. For PH, the principle is simple: no seat should go uncontested.
"That means no candidate should win uncontested. Otherwise, we disrupt the entire electoral process in this state election," he said.
He said it was crucial for every state seat to see at least a straight fight to give voters an opportunity to make a choice.
Meanwhile, a Bersatu source also indicated the possibility of seat clashes with PH, but declined to elaborate.
1cb0b41065cb7013: Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty ImagesThe Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive. With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since. The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote. What can we take away from the election results? The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote. Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way. What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes. The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government. Likud supporters at an election night event in Jerusalem, Israel. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory. It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government. Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election. What drove the Arab parties’ surprise showing? The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important. Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them. The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties. Israeli left-wing protesters call for the formation of a government including Arab parties. Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc. But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority. Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack. Was the vote a referendum on Netanyahu? Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel. But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings. Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States. But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption. Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat. What should we expect next? The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer. The party with the largest number of seats typically gets the first chance to assemble a governing coalition, but not always. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will choose who gets the first chance to form a government based on who is most likely to succeed. Right now, it looks like Eisenkot will get the first opportunity, but his only real option is to form a minority government that would depend on the parliamentary support of the Arab-majority parties – which some members of his Change Bloc adamantly oppose. Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag as he addresses supporters on Oct. 28, 2026. Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images Despite the success of the Arab-majority parties in the election, it is unlikely they will be invited to be formal members of any coalition – although that has happened once in the past, when the United Arab List joined the short-lived government of 2021-22 led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. If Eisenkot is unable to form a government, then Netanyahu will get the chance. He could try to entice some leaders of the parties in the Change bloc to defect and join a right-wing government under his leadership, or a broader “national unity” government with a rotating leader. Netanyahu did that in the past with Benny Gantz, but then he later prevented Gantz from becoming prime minister – so I doubt Eisenkot would agree to do this with Netanyahu. There are reports in the media that the Trump administration would like a national unity government in Israel, so that might increase the pressure on Eisenkot to accept this outcome. And should war with Iran heat up again, that would increase the pressure. The most likely scenario, I believe, is that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot will be able to form a government, and a new election will be called, with Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister until that vote. Netanyahu has reason to hope that his bloc will do better in another election, so that may well be his game plan. In which case, it will be many months until Israel has a new government. 26ef725b8d7c4480: KUALA LUMPUR: CTOS Digital Bhd is expected to report weaker fourth-quarter earnings as cybersecurity-related service disruptions and higher tax expenses weigh on profitability, according to CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd.
Analyst Mohd Shanaz Noor Azam said the temporary suspension of selected credit reporting services following the incident in late September could affect about 35 per cent of the company's revenue.
The disruption is expected to result in revenue losses and additional remediation costs, while transaction volumes could take 30 to 60 days to fully recover once services resume.
Shanaz said the expiry of CTOS's tax incentive on Nov 8 would add to earnings pressure, with taxable income becoming subject to the statutory corporate tax rate of 24 per cent.
This compares with the company's effective tax rate of 8.4 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.
"We expect these factors to weigh on fourth-quarter profitability, with the full impact of the higher tax rate becoming more pronounced in financial year 2027 (FY27)," he said in a note.
CIMB Securities maintained its "Hold" call on CTOS with a target price of 55 sen, pending the company's analyst briefing today.
The briefing is expected to provide greater clarity on the restoration of affected services and the recovery in transaction volumes.

Shanaz noted that CTOS had initially targeted resuming services in the third week of October, with each additional week of disruption potentially reducing profit after tax and minority interests by RM1.3 million.
He cautioned that prolonged disruptions could lead to customer losses, higher cybersecurity costs and further earnings pressure.
CIMB Securities said the successful restoration of affected services and a recovery in transaction volumes would be key catalysts for a potential re-rating of CTOS shares.

Other potential catalysts include stronger adoption of digital and alternative credit scoring solutions, cross-selling opportunities in Southeast Asia and possible special dividends from non-core asset disposals.

However, downside risks remain, including prolonged disruptions to Central Credit Reference Information System-related services, customers switching to competing credit bureaus and higher cybersecurity and compliance costs.
Other risks include slower sales conversion in the financial institution and corporate segment, further data breaches and adverse regulatory developments.
3fe408b735c39121: OCTOBER 29 — In the case of Dato’ Seri Anwar Bin Ibrahim v Perdana Menteri Malaysia [2007], the former Deputy Prime Minister (the Plaintiff) sued the Prime Minister and another (the Defendants) by way of an originating summons (OS) for a declaration that they had acted in contravention of the Federal Constitution in dismissing him as Deputy Prime Minister and that he was still a Minister in the Malaysian Cabinet.
The Defendants applied to strike out the Plaintiff’s claim under Order 18 rule 19(1) of the then Rules of High Court 1980 (now Rules of Court 2012).

One of the grounds advanced by the Defendants was the use of an incorrect procedure. It was argued that the Plaintiff’s action should be by way of an application for judicial review under Order 53 rather than by OS.
The High Court allowed the application of the Defendants, striking out the Plaintiff’s action.
Dissatisfied, the Plaintiff appealed to the Court of Appeal. After hearing the parties, the Court dismissed the appeal. Court of Appeal Judge Helilah (as she then was) said:

“This suit raises public law issues as it is a decision and action taken by the Prime Minister in pursuance of the provisions of the Federal Constitution that is being impugned. As such, a decision taken by the Prime Minister with regard to a Minister as a member of the administration in his public duties is one that has implications for the public as a whole, and it is in consequence of this that the public law is concerned with the decision-making process.
According to the author, when an explicit procedure is created, follow it or your action can be struck off. — Picture by Raymond Manuel

“The legal sources of the powers that are being impugned are in the public domain. As such, to institute the proceedings by [OS], though seemingly appearing to be simple in procedure, will deprive the public authority, in this case, the Federal Government and in the circumstances of the present case, of the protection of the law that is entitled to by the process available under Order 53.”

The Court of Appeal’s decision was cited with approval by the Federal Court in the case of Ahmad Jefri Mohd Jahri v. Pengarah Kebudayaan & Kesenian Johor & Ors [2010] where the apex court made it clear that the procedure to challenge the exercise of statutory powers by public authority has been explicitly provided under Order 53.

“As a general rule, an application for reliefs against public authority … which involves the question of the proper exercise of the statutory powers of the defendants as a public authority, should have proceeded under that rule [that is, Order 53]. The failure of which should stand the suit liable to be struck out.”
The apex court added as follows:

“Aside from mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari, or any others described under [Order 53], an alternative remedy for an aggrieved party seeking relief against a public authority on his infringed right to which he was entitled to protection under public law is for a declaration.

“However, [Order 53] sets out a specific procedure for an aggrieved party seeking relief, including a declaration, against a public authority on his infringed right to which he was entitled to protection under public law to follow.

“It is our view that when such an explicit procedure is created to cater to this purpose, then, as a general rule, all such applications for such relief must commence according to what is set down in [Order 53]; otherwise, it would be liable to be struck off for abusing the process of the court.”
When an explicit procedure is created, follow it or your action can be struck off.

69760f927eb1f76a: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's total fertility rate (TFR) remains below the replacement level, recording 1.6 children per woman aged 15 to 49 in 2024.
National Population and Family Development Board (LPPKN) director-general Datuk Abdul Shukur Abdullah said the rate was well below the population replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.
"Based on the Vital Statistics Malaysia 2025 report published by the Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM), Malaysia's TFR for 2024 stood at 1.6 children for every woman aged 15 to 49.
"This rate is far below the population replacement level, which is around 2.1 children per woman," he said.
By ethnic group, the Malay community recorded the highest TFR in 2024 at 1.9 children per woman, followed by other Bumiputeras at 1.6, Indians at 1.1, and Chinese at 0.9.
He said that while the Chinese community recorded the lowest fertility rate, the trend should not be linked solely to cultural or racial factors.

"Among the factors influencing low fertility are delayed marriages, an increasing age when having the first child, living and housing costs, childcare and education expenses, higher female participation in education and employment, and challenges in balancing work and family responsibilities," he said.
He said couples in urban areas were also more cautious about family planning.

"The decision to have a second or third child does not depend merely on the desire to have children, but on whether the family has sufficient time, financial resources, childcare support, and workplace backing," he said.
He said Malaysia must intensify interventions to slow the declining fertility rate to prevent population decline and age-structure imbalances by 2100.
Abdul Shukur said the national TFR dropped from 2.0 children per woman in 2015 to 1.6 in 2024.
The drop was far below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman, which is the level needed to maintain population size over the long term without taking migration into account, he said.

"However, declining fertility is not unique to Malaysia. It is a global trend, especially in developed countries where more women pursue higher education, enter the workforce, and postpone marriage and childbearing.
"Malaysia is among the countries experiencing a rapid decline in fertility rates. Looking at the data from 2015 to 2024, the rate fell by 0.4 points in about 10 years.
"Therefore, interventions must be carried out to slow this trend so that we can delay population decline," he said.
On long-term targets, Abdul Shukur said demographic studies showed Malaysia was unlikely to meet its previously projected target of 70 million people by 2100.
He said Malaysia must address changes in its population structure caused by declining birth rates and rising life expectancy.
"This situation can lead to an increase in the elderly population compared with the youth, which will strain social support systems, healthcare, and retirement savings.
"With the fertility rate at 1.6, we must look at the long-term impact.
"If births continue to fall behind deaths, the population could begin to shrink," he said.
On efforts to boost fertility rates, Abdul Shukur said it was not an easy task as it required substantial investment and a comprehensive approach to ease the cost of raising children.

"The experience of several countries that have succeeded in raising fertility rates shows that governments must provide financial support and facilities that enable couples to balance work and family life.
"The government needs to invest in reducing the cost of raising children, including financial aid, childcare, and family support.
"When couples are forced to choose between building careers and having children, costs and support facilities become key considerations," he said.
He noted that several states had introduced childbirth and family-related assistance, but their capacity to offer incentives varied depending on their financial standing.

"Therefore, efforts to raise fertility cannot rely solely on baby bonuses. They must be supported by a family-friendly ecosystem that encompasses childcare, education, and work-life balance," he said.
Abdul Shukur also said preparations for an ageing population must be prioritised, including ensuring that senior citizens have adequate retirement savings and strong family support systems.
He said longer life expectancy meant people must prepare financially and physically for extended retirement years.
"Ageing is not just about population figures. We must also look at physical and mental health, financial capacity, and family support.
"Family ties are essential so that the elderly are not marginalised or forced to live alone without support," he said.
Abdul Shukur added that strong family foundations must be established before marriage and maintained throughout family life to foster love, responsibility, and mutual support.
