ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the views of SSRI or Penn State.
1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest. 04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. 119cf39f6711bef0: Many of the stores where people use SNAP benefits are small. O2O Creative/E+ via Getty ImagesAfter 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change. That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal. SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited. States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts. In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits. We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country. We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant. Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%. Why it matters Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining. Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets. Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program. Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking. What still isn’t known We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program. We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue. Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold. Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores. Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied. a94cb7158a379b67: Amber Titus, 38, holds a take-home dose of methadone on Sept. 18 in Bisbee Junction, Ariz. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-NDThree times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic. Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025. “It’s been a godsend,” she said. But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home. The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m. Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open. Like many people with opioid use disorder, Amber Titus struggles to access methadone treatment. Three times a week, she drives 45 minutes each way with her 1-year-old son in his car seat to get the medication. Here’s her story. That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic. “They said they’d be at my house at 6 o'clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said. Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it. For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities. Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care. I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities. This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety. Why methadone fits the private equity model Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly. In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so. Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply. That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication. Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms. In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply. To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator. Market share grew, methadone supply didn’t My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs. Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it. Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period. In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed. As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners. Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone. Amber Titus, 38, leaves her appointment at Community Medical Services’ methadone clinic in Sierra Vista, Ariz., on Sept. 18. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open. Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units. Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said. No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said. Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging. But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens. For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose. A proposal to expand methadone access These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs. The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term. Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027. In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic. “I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.” Methadone for opioid use disorder is typically taken orally, most often as a liquid. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk. The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out. Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form. Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment. Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug. “We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it. Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further. “It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email. The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it. “They don’t have to die,” she said. Bringing private equity deals into view Two other policy responses are gaining traction. The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies. Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony. The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county. The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close. Structural barriers to getting treatment The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. In 2024, federal data shows the number of people who died from drug overdoses declined to nearly 80,000, and more than 54,000 of those deaths involved opioids. We already have medications that work. The barriers preventing people from accessing them are not primarily clinical. They are structural – and, in this case, actively maintained by financial investors who profit from the status quo. 7f9e54d5ff79b396: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models

When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.

He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.
Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.
—Matthew King
Are we there yet? Interspecies communication
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.

Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.
Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.
—Cassandra Willyard

This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

9f576285187c230f: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse.

It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification.
Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool?
“But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register.

She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags.
“And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said.

“Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.”

Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories.

Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication

“A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both."
Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.

In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack.
For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said.

The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file:

While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans.
For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox.
“The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said.
“Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.”

According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them.

“The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.”

The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote.
Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said.
“Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®
a7f329bb1936cd9a: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data.

Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised.

A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected.
123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker.

"Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said.

"Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts."

They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in.
There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too.

"The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us.

"In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked.
"That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us."

The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU.

The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners."

123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification.
The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution.

"If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone.

"We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account.
"We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

085f662b6c506ab0: The question of who controls satellite-based connectivity came into sharp focus in recent weeks after Ukraine's service was throttled and then restored.

Wherever Reg readers stand on those activities involving SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield, reliance on a foreign power that may not stay friendly is now under intense scrutiny. Alternatives exist, including Eutelsat OneWeb's constellation, and more are in the works. The Register toured the Harwell facility of another contender – Open Cosmos.

The business is just over a decade old and operates from multiple locations, including the UK, Greece, and Portugal. It has launched dozens of missions over the years, including its OpenConstellation service, which organizations use to share data from Earth observation satellites.

When it launched OpenConstellation in 2022, the aim was to have 25 satellites offering a mix of spatial and spectral resolution. While other services, such as the European Commission's Copernicus, provide similar data, OpenConstellation lets customers assign satellites specific tasks for specific data collection.

However, it is ConnectedCosmos that will interest users concerned about putting all their connectivity eggs in a basket that might be abruptly snatched away. The first two satellites in the constellation are now in orbit; they were launched by Rocket Lab in January 2026. The business plans to operate more than 96 satellites by the end of 2028 and to achieve full coverage by 2030. The core connectivity backbone will consist of 192 satellites, which founder and CEO Rafel Jordà Siquier described as "the foundation, not the ceiling."

The company reckons it can churn out one satellite per day, and judging by what we saw in Harwell, that figure seems realistic, though it's a far cry from the approximately 70 Starlinks per week SpaceX claimed in its IPO filing.
Because ConnectedCosmos operates from an altitude above 1,000 km, it needs far fewer satellites, though at the cost of latency increases.

Jordi Barrera Ars, co-founder and CTO, told us that latency was "anything between 30 and 80 milliseconds." This is OK for most applications, but not great for some. Direct to smartphone is, for example, not currently on the cards. Open Cosmos's VP of Commercial Satcom, Danielle Edwards, said, "We're very much in the direct device business. Direct to smartphone is not an area that we have an interest in right now."
"Never say never…" she added, "and who knows what might come along next Tuesday. But for right now, the direct device play really is on the IoT side."

During the tour, Open Cosmos showed off its assembly and testing facilities (including temperature and pressure testing), as well as a shaker table that simulates launch conditions. The satellites themselves consist of a common bus, onto which solar panels and the payload are fitted. Then they are stored, ready for launch, in what one company representative called "the satellite nursery".

The approach is interesting: OpenConstellation satellites use the ConnectedCosmos constellation as a connectivity backbone, while the latter also provides point-to-point broadband. According to Open Cosmos:
"The constellation is deliberately designed around the requirements of government, institutional and commercial customers that need secure, resilient connectivity and clear custody of critical data."
It is very much a European alternative to customers who are worried about existing services.

The service on offer from Open Cosmos will not, for example, be suitable for guiding drones traveling at high velocities, that isn't really the point, but it will provide sovereign communication channels that aren't beholden to the whim of a man and a big, red Off switch. Where the Starlink constellation stands at well over 10,000 satellites, the numbers proposed by Open Cosmos are far more modest and less likely to alarm astronomers in quite the same way.

Plus, the company has sector experience through its OpenConstellation platform (as well as custom spacecraft built for individual customers). And, unlike so many in the industry, its satellites and facilities exist beyond PowerPoint presentations. After all, we've seen them. ®
c3dd7b56c8c9e3cf: After suffering more than 10,000 corporate meetings, one executive has decided that the world hasn't endured nearly enough management jargon and built an app capable of generating 270 million variations of it.

Dave Doty, who claims to have spent 35 years collecting buzzwords, clichés, and other verbal atrocities inflicted on office workers, turned his life's work into Executive Eightball, an iPhone and Android app designed to help users sound convincingly corporate while saying nothing.
The idea came about after Doty spent decades recording the nonsense he heard in meetings, presumably while everyone else was busy circling back, touching base, and taking things offline.

"I am an executive who has suffered through over 10,000 meetings during the course of my 30-year career," Doty told The Register. "To keep my sanity, in each of them, I wrote down all of the buzz words and business clichés and have built an enormous database of them."
He described his creation as "sort of what would happen if Dilbert and George Costanza had a love child."

The app, which is now available on Apple's App Store and Google Play, takes Doty's collection of corporate waffle and assembles it into sentences that wouldn't look out of place in a CEO's quarterly update or a particularly painful all-hands meeting.

Among the pearls of wisdom it can produce are "We must dashboard the outputs to enable us to focus on operational directives and break the paradigm" and "Drive to cross-functional synergies so we can reengineer the organization and unleash shareholder value."

Doty claims Executive Eightball can produce approximately 270 million unique sentences in 15 languages, meaning workers across the globe can now contribute to meetings without the tiresome business of having an actual idea.

The app's listing promises to help users "Speak fluent corporate nonsense instantly," with suggested applications including office humor, LinkedIn jokes, presentation icebreakers, and, perhaps most appropriately, "Fake CEO energy."
There's a free version, although you'll have to put up with ads and a limited supply of corporate waffle. For $0.99, you can unlock the lot and talk complete rubbish to your heart's content.

The timing is rather fitting. In March, research covered by The Register suggested that people who enthusiastically embrace corporate buzzwords may actually be worse at their jobs. Now there's an app to help the rest of us catch up.
Doty, meanwhile, appears delighted with his contribution to the corporate world.

"This is truly a paradigm shift for corporate leadership and my greatest lifetime contribution to society," he wrote in his latest email, urging potential customers to subscribe to the paid version to "unleash the value."
After 35 years and 10,000 meetings, at least someone has finally found a productive use for all that wasted time. ®

4edc65ce2580159a: Newly formed Quake AI is a cloud provider that expects its users will be mostly agents rather than humans.

It was created after US-based Rumble Inc acquired German datacenter operator Northern Data in June. The parent then rebranded as RUM Group, a holding company for Quake AI (formerly Northern Data) and the Rumble video platform.
Quake AI is an Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP) operating a 22,000 GPUs estate, making it a neocloud: a specialized infrastructure provider dedicated to AI workloads.

Yet where other neoclouds are building a full stack of services around their GPU farms, Quake AI wants to make its infrastructure discoverable to AI agents, which may soon be traversing the internet in hordes on behalf of their owners.
RUM Group's chief financial officer Mike Massey told The Register that "Cloud 1.0 - let's call it applications - is like a user interface of how you interact with a machine of some kind."

He added: "Now, if you think about agents, they don't use vision. That's not how they interact with systems. They interact with APIs and with information effectively, and that means they want highly discoverable, highly data-driven platforms..

“So, to us, the things that make GPUs and AI compute easier to consume for humans, things like model-as-a-service, dashboards and one-click settings, are actually orthogonal to, if not detrimental to what agents are going to want, agents are going to want homogeneous compute… to understand and know what your data and your expectations are in terms of performance and uptimes, and then they're going to want to consume that compute as a utility,” he claimed.
In other words, Quake AI believes that, at some point, the customers for its compute services are going to be AI agents rather than people, but carrying out tasks on their behalf.
“I think that is the case, and it's the vision that we are driving towards, and you know ultimately agents are in service of people, right?” Massey said.

In its view of things, agents won't go through an intermediary, they'll go to the compute to retrieve the answers they need. "So all of these tool frameworks and all of these things that we have set up, I think, are a hindrance or an encumbrance to what the agents are going to want to consume, which is a utility," he explained.

"Yes, we're a little crazy in this regard," Massey added. "It's different. But I think our worldview is very grounded in the data and the realities. Like, we're a technical team. We understand the engineering, and at the end of the day, I think that most would validate our hypothesis," he continued.
John Hoffman, CEO of Northern Data and acting CEO of Quake AI, compared this with a solution he had been shown of an AI that was developed to navigate the internet by itself.

"I told it I wanted pizza. It went on to DoorDash's website. Typed pizza in the search box, clicked on the pizza with the highest ranking, went to add to order, knows I like pepperoni, and it clicked through all of this," he said.

"Don't get me wrong, this was a good solution that solves the problem. But the amount of compute that you are using to try to get an AI agent to act like a human that has eyes that can see web links is insanity compared to if DoorDash just created an API that is queryable," Hoffman claimed.

Done that way, the compute usage would be one thousandth of the way that the problem was actually accomplished, Quake AI claims, but it will require that everybody embraces the idea of how agents interact.
"And they don't interact with interfaces or applications. They interact with data and APIs. Just give me the raw data. That's what it wants," Hoffman told us.
"I would imagine DoorDash is developing an API for agents," he added. "It just makes sense, and that’s why we're doing the same exact thing."

Earlier this year, TollBit, an outfit that tracks AI bot traffic, said that agents were gradually taking over the internet. Its State of the Bots report found that by the end of 2025, there was roughly one AI bot visit for every 31 human visits to a site, up from just one for every 200 human visits at the start of the year.

Last year, consultants McKinsey & Company produced a report saying that the neocloud operators had to evolve beyond being just a provider of GPUs-as-a-service and move up the AI stack to sell services on top of bare metal, or risk being commoditized into competing on price.

Analyst firm Gartner was also reading the last rites for much of the neocloud industry recently, forecasting that AI services are unlikely to deliver enough revenue to cover the expected capital expenditure on IT infrastructure between now and 2030, and that consolidation in the provider market was inevitable.

Quake AI's gamble is that AI agents will be a reality, and that by tailoring its APIs to make it easier for these autonomous software bots to access its resources as needed, it will be one of the winners. ®

dee1398ef25eba6c: Travelling in the modern day and age differs significantly from what it looked like a few short decades ago. Today, it is all about apps: you need applications for navigation, booking accommodation, buying tickets for events, following the local news, staying in touch with friends and family, and more. That also means that you depend on connectivity at all times while abroad.

The problem is that a lot of people still rely on traditional roaming, while the roaming model is out of date. You cannot choose a specific mobile internet plan that suits your travel plans. Instead, operators have split the world into zones, and each zone has its own pricing, limits, and permissions.

That is why many have turned to alternative ways of staying connected, and so far, the travel eSIM has emerged as the most practical solution. Companies like the Swiss eSIM pioneer, Yesim, have recognized the problem that travelers are facing and have come up with a solution. They let you pick a specific plan that will fit your trip. That way, you get to tailor your connectivity experience in advance. Furthermore, you even get to see the price in advance and know exactly what you will have to pay.
Home-operator roaming: Connectivity under outdated rules

The problem with roaming is that your home operator decides what your internet will be like abroad. When you try to book a flight or a hotel room, you will try to get the best deal possible. That means comparing providers, prices, any potential benefits that different providers offer, and the like. However, with roaming, you can’t do any of that. The terms of your existing home contract still apply, and connectivity abroad just gets added to it.

That means that your operator decides what zones are available, what partner networks you can access, and, most importantly, how much they will charge you. You, as the user, can only accept their terms or choose to look for a different way to secure an internet connection. In other words, there is no flexibility and no participation on your end, you can only take it or leave it.

Take EE as an example - the official terms for their EE Travel Data pass for Canada and the US say that the user gets 500 MB of data per day. This is not nearly enough for someone who will depend on their phone for everything, from paying for food to comparing ticket prices and booking accommodation. The limit is the same for countless other countries, including Australia, China, India, Mexico, New Zealand, South Africa, Thailand, Turkey, and the UAE.

It gets even worse for other countries, including Japan, Singapore, South Korea, and Indonesia. For these, the daily allowance is only 150 MB. That essentially forces you to ration your data use very carefully and pick what you are going to use it for.

Some providers have introduced daily packages as a secondary roaming option. O2 Travel Bolt On roaming option for Pay Monthly customers charges £7 for every 24 hours of use. They start charging you as soon as you make a call, send a text, or use data for anything. It happens even if your phone updates an app automatically in the background, without you even knowing about it.

As a result, you get barely any connectivity, but still have to pay the full price of this deal. For some, that might be fine, but if you aren’t aware of it, you can return home to a surprise bill that you now have to pay.
Travel eSIM as an alternative to roaming: Choice and control pass to the user
As mentioned, travel eSIM emerged as an alternative to the roaming model. The first thing to note about it is the difference between an eSIM and a travel eSIM.

An eSIM is a chip that is built into most modern smartphones, tablets, and similar devices. This chip allows users to install operator profiles offered by travel eSIM providers. This can be done remotely, without having to go to the provider’s shop. It’s as simple as downloading an app.

Travel eSIM uses this chip to create a digital service. That typically includes the provider’s app, tariffs, partnered mobile networks, full control of your data, and even top-ups and customer support, should you need them.

The system is also quite practical, as you get to set up everything in advance. You don’t have to wait to enter another country to secure your connectivity, but can instead do it from home before you leave on your trip. Start by checking your device’s compatibility with eSIM technology. If it’s compatible, you can download the operator’s app, pick a package for the region you plan to visit, and install the appropriate profile. Then, sit on the plane, travel to your destination, and activate the profile when you get there. You get instant connectivity without having to stand in line at a SIM kiosk, rely on Wi-Fi coverage, or pay high roaming prices.

If you are still not sure if a travel eSIM is the right option, consider the following: A one-week trip from the UK to the US will have you paying £7 per day if you are an O2 Travel user. For seven days abroad, that will end up being £49. Alternatively, if you use Yesim’s unlimited package for the US for seven days, the price is only £18.27 as of the time of writing. You buy it upfront, and it won’t activate until you start using it after arriving at your destination.
Travel eSIM fits the app-first logic of travel

When selecting a plan, you start with the trip itself. In other words, you click on the country or region that you plan to visit. You can also enter the length of your stay there, and how much data you expect you will need. Then, select a tariff to match the parameters.

All terms of the deal will be known to you in advance, including the country that is covered by the plan, how long the plan will last, how much data you get, and how much it all costs. Best of all, everything is managed in the app, so you don’t really have to get in contact with anyone.

A package can be selected for a single country, an entire region, or a route that includes several countries. You prepare all of this at home, and activate it after arrival. You even get to keep your home number active, since you don’t have to replace your SIM card. That way, any banking messages, service notifications, important calls, 2-Factor Authentication (2FA) texts, and the like can come through and reach you at any time.
Yesim: The Swiss standard for travel connectivity

If you need a travel eSIM provider, consider the Swiss company Yesim. The firm has been in the travel eSIM market since 2019, becoming one of the pioneers in this sector. Today, it provides connectivity to over 4 million users across 200+ destinations. For travelers, this means that they can rely on one service that they are familiar with regardless of whether they are going on a short holiday in one country or a lengthy, complex trip that will include multiple nations.

Yesim’s position as a global provider of connectivity services is also reflected in the fact that the company has become an official partner of the World Players Super League - the largest golf tour in the world. The League holds over 1,800 tournaments in more than 50 countries every year, and is one of the largest events of this kind.

The same global scale is evident in Yesim’s pricing options. The firm offers a flexible tariff range, especially when it comes to its most popular packages. For example, the Global Package covers 80+ countries, while the Global Plus Package covers 140+ destinations. These will likely suit those who tend to travel a lot and want to pay a fixed budget. But, if your data needs are unpredictable, you can always pick the Pay & Fly tariff - Yesim’s pay-as-you-go model. This is a single eSIM for 170+ countries, and you only pay for the data that you actually used.

Yesim’s offer is known for the ease and simplicity of connection. The firm has created an intuitive app where you simply pick a country or a region, install the profile, and activate it in a few taps after getting there. Plus, the app uses automatic network selection. This is possible thanks to SwitchLess Networks technology, which switches the user to the strongest available network at any given time. This is especially important for remote locations, where connectivity is usually unstable, but it can also come in handy for mass events, when the network may struggle to cope with tens of thousands of connections at once.

Yesim also offers the Multiple eSIMs feature, which helps you manage several profiles from a single account. This is convenient for those traveling with their family or a small group. You can even test its service with a trial plan that gives you 500 MB for a symbolic price of £0.45. That way, you can see how it all works for yourself before committing any real money. Lastly, Yesim offers a 15 percent discount to new users who use promocode GETYESIM15, so make sure to use it.
Conclusion

Since modern travel has evolved and is now an app-first experience, the old roaming model is no longer a good fit for an average traveler. Instead, travel eSIMs give tourists the freedom to choose their location, amount of data, and even to know the cost upfront. Yesim is a prime example of the fact that the travel eSIM model works and that it can satisfy the needs of modern-day travellers.

"For Yesim, freedom of connectivity is a fundamental human right that helps people stay close, communicate, and share meaningful moments in spite of distance," emphasizes the company's founder and CEO, Dmitri Verbovski.
